allObjections.title: §7.6 readiness mis-scored
allObjections.detail: GTM Readiness Report (§7.6) subtracts by finding counts across the whole product, but the current assessment path only crawls a single page (consultation fact 3). This produces artificially inflated scores that still feed Clearance Step 5 (§11), risking green-lighting products that were not fully assessed.

allObjections.title: Bypassing Agent #21 ownership
allObjections.detail: SSOT §15.1 assigns the Aggressive Crawl Conductor to Agent #21 and §15.3 requires routing via OrchestratorHub, with audit topics in §14.1 (e.g., 21.crawl.completed.v1). The assessment path calls a direct single-page `crawl()` (consultation fact 3) and never emits the §21 topics, violating the conductor/instrument separation and creating audit blind spots.

allObjections.title: §7 ProductSSOT atomicity not upheld
allObjections.detail: Output Contract item #5 requires ProductSSOT updates to be atomic with outputs, including architecture snapshot updates that ACE would generate. With aggressiveCrawl() not wired into the 8-step assessment (consultation facts 2–3), the `architecture_snapshot` and `governance_record` entries (gtm_readiness_score) are not consistently written, undermining rollback semantics and the symbiotic loop in §28.

allObjections.title: Credential handling gap vs §6
allObjections.detail: §6 mandates authenticated traversal with strict `scrubCredentials()` and ephemeral `storageState` deletion. Consultation fact 4 confirms auth traversal is unbuilt; when added ad hoc to assessment, the absence of the §6 guardrails risks session bleed or credentials appearing in screenshots/network logs contrary to §14.3 PII-scrub guarantees.

allObjections.title: Cost-governance bypass risk
allObjections.detail: ACE has a $15/run budget and per-product cap via Doppler (§7.6). If multi-page crawling is wired into assessment without Agent #21’s chartered ownership and budget enforcement, assessments may exceed cost ceilings unpredictably, breaching §8 cost-aware ranking and the stated crawl budget contract.

allObjections.title: Credential handling security gap
allObjections.detail: §6 specifies credential handling via scrubCredentials() but the implementation fact #4 states 'no execution path performs an authenticated multi-page crawl.' This means the credential scrubbing code is untested in production, creating a critical security surface when auth is eventually wired.

allObjections.title: Agent #21 dormancy blocks SSOT compliance
allObjections.detail: §15.1 row 21 assigns Aggressive Crawl Conductor ownership to Agent #21, but fact #5 confirms it's DORMANT with no class file. The SSOT requires agent-based orchestration, yet the actual aggressiveCrawl() function bypasses the agent layer entirely, violating the architectural contract.

allObjections.title: Cost ceiling enforcement missing
allObjections.detail: §7.6 specifies a $15/run/product/environment cost ceiling for aggressive crawls, but the shipped aggressiveCrawl() function has no cost tracking or circuit breaker. At depth=8/pages=200, a single uncapped crawl could consume hundreds of dollars.

allObjections.title: Lack of clarity
allObjections.detail: The proposal under review lacks clear definitions of key terms, such as 'full-product scope' and 'single-page assessment', which could lead to confusion and misinterpretation. For example, §6 of the canonical SSOT specifies a full-product multi-page authenticated crawl, but the codebase only implements a single-page crawl.

allObjections.title: Inconsistent implementation
allObjections.detail: The implementation of the crawl functionality is inconsistent, with the renewal pipeline using a multi-page engine and the assessment pipeline using a single-page engine. This inconsistency could lead to incorrect or incomplete assessments. Specifically, the `aggressiveCrawl()` function in `src/lib/crawler.js` is only wired to the renewal pipeline, not the assessment pipeline.

allObjections.title: Unbuilt authenticated traversal
allObjections.detail: The proposal acknowledges that authenticated traversal is unbuilt, which could limit the effectiveness of the full-product crawl. Without authenticated traversal, the crawl may not be able to access gated content, leading to incomplete assessments. For instance, the `aggressiveCrawl()` function does not handle authenticated sessions, which could result in missed issues.

allObjections.title: Unclear Dependency Management
allObjections.detail: §3 mentions dependency management but does not specify how dependencies are managed or updated. This could lead to version conflicts and security vulnerabilities.

allObjections.title: Overlapping Agent Roles
allObjections.detail: §15.1 lists agents with overlapping responsibilities, such as Agent #3 and Agent #26 both handling self-renewal tasks. This overlap could lead to conflicts and inefficiencies.

allObjections.title: Incomplete Security Measures
allObjections.detail: §20 mentions several security measures, but it does not address how data encryption is handled during transmission and storage. This is a critical oversight for data security.

allObjections.title: Lack of Clear Governance
allObjections.detail: §19 outlines governance mechanisms, but it does not specify how conflicts between the 95/95 score threshold and the 6-step Product Clearance Protocol are resolved. This could lead to inconsistent decision-making.

allObjections.title: Lack of clarity on implementation
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not provide a clear implementation plan for the full-product crawl and authenticated traversal. It is not clear how the existing engine will be wired into the assessment pipeline, and how Agent #21 will be registered.

allObjections.title: Potential security risks
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not address the security risks associated with authenticated traversal, such as credential storage, session bleed, and accidental data exfiltration via crawl. This could lead to potential data breaches and security vulnerabilities.

allObjections.title: Unvalidated scoring engine
allObjections.detail: The scoring engine has not been validated on multi-page input, which could lead to inaccurate quality metrics and potential issues with the product assessment.

allObjections.title: Unbuilt authenticated traversal
allObjections.detail: §6 specifies authenticated session handling for crawls, but the codebase lacks implementation (fact 4). This renders full-product assessments impossible for gated content, violating the Aggressive Crawl Engine's scope. Without credential hydration, key user flows remain untested despite §6 claims.

allObjections.title: Agent #21 dormant wiring
allObjections.detail: §15.1 designates Agent #21 as the Aggressive Crawl Conductor, but it remains unwired and dormant. The existing renewal pipeline's multi-page crawler isn't integrated into the 8-step assessment path (fact 5), creating a structural gap between specification and execution that undermines §6's crawl guarantees.

allObjections.title: Misrepresentation risk
allObjections.detail: Assessments generated from single-page crawls (fact 3) are presented without scope disclaimers, contradicting §7.6's GTM Readiness Report requirements. This violates §11 Clearance Step 5 integrity by implying full-product coverage where none exists, potentially misleading stakeholders.

allObjections.title: Cost escalation unaddressed
allObjections.detail: Wiring §6's aggressive crawl to assessments activates its $15/run cost ceiling without solving §7.6's cost-aware narrowing mechanics. For products with 200+ pages, frequent assessments could breach budgets since §28.2's delta-crawl optimization requires stable ProductSSOT—unavailable for new products.

allObjections.title: Auth path is absent
allObjections.detail: §6 requires authenticated traversal with session hydration and retry logic, but the proposal itself admits no code path performs an authenticated multi-page crawl. That means the proposed “wire it into assessment” work is not a simple reroute; it requires building a new credential-handling surface with failure modes that are not covered by the current spec or shipping tests.

allObjections.title: Assessment semantics diverge
allObjections.detail: The 8-step assessment pipeline currently uses `api/research-url.js` single-page crawl output, while §6 describes a broader renewal-time engine with click sweeps, modal probing, and AI-agent probing. Replacing the assessment path with aggressive crawl changes the meaning of historical scores, so any trendline or clearance gating built on prior homepage-only results becomes apples-to-oranges unless the report schema/versioning is explicitly revised.

allObjections.title: Agent ownership is unresolved
allObjections.detail: The proposal says Agent #21 owns the Aggressive Crawl Conductor role, but also states it is dormant with no class file shipped and no `registerAgent()` call wired. Wiring aggressive crawl first without canonical agent registration creates a governance hole: the system would be using a capability that the SSOT treats as owned by an unshipped agent, which risks bypassing the agent-layer accountability model in §15.

allObjections.title: §6 crawl scope vs crawler.js wiring
allObjections.detail: §6 mandates depth=8/pages=200 + 8 interaction passes (auth, click-everything, modal, AI-probe) for every product assessment, yet aggressiveCrawl() in src/lib/crawler.js lines 594–722 is wired exclusively to the renewal pipeline and the 8-step assessment path still calls the single-page crawl() in api/research-url.js line 23.

allObjections.title: §15.1 row 21 Agent #21 dormant
allObjections.detail: §15.1 declares Agent #21 Ops Runner Alpha as Aggressive Crawl Conductor owning the full spider with dual authority [recommend_only, auto_write_internal, requires_human_gate], but no class file, no registerAgent() call, and status remains DORMANT with 'wire-in pending'.

allObjections.title: §7.6 GTM Readiness scoring invalid
allObjections.detail: §7.6 defines the 100 − 10·crit − 5·high − 2·med − 0.5·low formula and four score bands that map to Clearance Step 5, yet all shipped assessment outputs derive from single-page homepage crawls, so the metric has never been validated on the multi-page input it assumes.

A pause for a foundation audit would reduce the chance of compounding hidden gaps into the scoring and clearance pipeline.

Q1.pick_text: Implementation gap — SSOT is sound; wire the engine that already exists.
Q1.rationale: §6, §7.6, and §15.1 are coherent; the code simply routes assessments through a single-page `crawl()` and leaves Agent #21 dormant (consultation facts 2–5). The remedy is wiring and auth implementation, not changing the spec.

Q2.pick_text: Defect — single-page output must not be presented as a product assessment until the full-product crawl is wired.
Q2.rationale: Clearance Step 5 (§11) depends on the GTM Readiness Report (§7.6) derived from full-product findings; presenting single-page as a product assessment misrepresents coverage and can falsely satisfy gates.

Q3.pick_text: Wire Agent #21 Ops Runner Alpha canonically first — per the SSOT §15.1 ownership row, not as a code shortcut around the agent layer.
Q3.rationale: This preserves §15.3’s conductor/instrument separation and enables correct audit topics (§14.1) and budget governance before adding depth and auth traversal.

Q4.pick_text: After — most dormant agents assume full-product input that does not yet exist; building on missing substrate is rework risk.
Q4.rationale: Agents like #8, #9, and #10 depend on whole-product signals (ACE + ProductSSOT). Shipping them against single-page inputs will force redesign once §6 is realized.

Q5.pick_text: Authenticated-traversal security: credential storage, session bleed, accidental data exfiltration via crawl.
Q5.rationale: Consultation fact 4 shows auth traversal is unbuilt; without §6’s scrubbing and ephemeral guarantees fully enforced, introducing auth is the highest-impact unmitigated risk.

Q6.pick_text: Proceed in defined phases with explicit gates — staged build, each phase Panel-or-CEO-reviewed before the next.
Q6.rationale: Phase 1: wire Agent #21 + audit topics and budget caps; Phase 2: multi-page integration into assessment; Phase 3: authenticated traversal; Phase 4: UI/reporting labels removal after full coverage. Each phase should close governance and security checks.

perReviewer.overallNotes: Ensure the UI/report explicitly labels current assessments as single-page until ACE + auth are live and audited; otherwise block Clearance Step 5.

Q4.pick_text: After — most dormant agents assume full-product input that does not yet exist; building on missing substrate is rework risk.
Q4.rationale: Building agents that expect full-product crawl data when only single-page data exists creates technical debt and false confidence in untested code paths.

Q5.pick_text: Authenticated-traversal security: credential storage, session bleed, accidental data exfiltration via crawl.
Q5.rationale: The combination of multi-tenant architecture, credential handling, and aggressive crawling creates a perfect storm for security incidents if session isolation isn't bulletproof.

Q6.pick_text: Proceed in defined phases with explicit gates — staged build, each phase Panel-or-CEO-reviewed before the next.
Q6.rationale: Given the security risks and architectural gaps, a phased approach with explicit review gates is the only responsible path forward.

perReviewer.overallNotes: The proposal correctly identifies an implementation gap but underestimates the security and architectural risks of proceeding without proper foundations.

objections.title: Unbuilt authenticated traversal
objections.detail: §6 specifies authenticated session handling for crawls, but the codebase lacks implementation (fact 4). This renders full-product assessments impossible for gated content, violating the Aggressive Crawl Engine's scope. Without credential hydration, key user flows remain untested despite §6 claims.

objections.title: Agent #21 dormant wiring
objections.detail: §15.1 designates Agent #21 as the Aggressive Crawl Conductor, but it remains unwired and dormant. The existing renewal pipeline's multi-page crawler isn't integrated into the 8-step assessment path (fact 5), creating a structural gap between specification and execution that undermines §6's crawl guarantees.

objections.title: Misrepresentation risk
objections.detail: Assessments generated from single-page crawls (fact 3) are presented without scope disclaimers, contradicting §7.6's GTM Readiness Report requirements. This violates §11 Clearance Step 5 integrity by implying full-product coverage where none exists, potentially misleading stakeholders.

objections.title: Cost escalation unaddressed
objections.detail: Wiring §6's aggressive crawl to assessments activates its $15/run cost ceiling without solving §7.6's cost-aware narrowing mechanics. For products with 200+ pages, frequent assessments could breach budgets since §28.2's delta-crawl optimization requires stable ProductSSOT—unavailable for new products.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: Implementing multi-page crawling without authentication (per Q3 option 2) would generate 'full-product' assessments that miss critical auth-gated flows (e.g., dashboards, payment screens). This creates false confidence compared to the current single-page assessments which at least accurately reflect their limited scope, leading to undetected failures in production environments.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The proposal should be rejected because wiring half-implemented crawl machinery risks institutionalizing technical debt. §6's auth requirements and Agent #21 dependencies reveal foundational gaps; proceeding without resolving these could produce assessments that are both more expensive and less reliable than the current single-page approach, violating Locked Rule 3's governance safeguards.

Q1.pick_text: Both — SSOT is sound in principle but parts of §6 are unbuildable as written.
Q1.rationale: §6's crawl specification is technically sound but relies on unbuilt auth and dormant agents, making it partially unimplementable in the current state.

Q2.pick_text: Acceptable interim only if the UI + report header explicitly label the output as single-page, not full-product.
Q2.rationale: Current outputs are useful for homepage checks but must not misrepresent scope; explicit labeling aligns with §14.1 audit transparency requirements.

Q3.pick_text: Build authenticated traversal first — depth without auth has limited value on real apps that gate content behind login.
Q3.rationale: Auth is §6's core gap; without it, multi-page crawls miss critical paths, undermining the assessment value proposition entirely.

Q5.pick_text: Authenticated-traversal security: credential storage, session bleed, accidental data exfiltration via crawl.

Q6.rationale: Phased implementation (e.g., auth→Agent#21→crawl wiring) with governance checkpoints balances progress with risk mitigation per Locked Rule 17.

perReviewer.overallNotes: Prioritize auth implementation before any crawl scope expansion to prevent systemic integrity erosion.

objections.title: Auth path is absent
objections.detail: §6 requires authenticated traversal with session hydration and retry logic, but the proposal itself admits no code path performs an authenticated multi-page crawl. That means the proposed “wire it into assessment” work is not a simple reroute; it requires building a new credential-handling surface with failure modes that are not covered by the current spec or shipping tests.

objections.title: Assessment semantics diverge
objections.detail: The 8-step assessment pipeline currently uses `api/research-url.js` single-page crawl output, while §6 describes a broader renewal-time engine with click sweeps, modal probing, and AI-agent probing. Replacing the assessment path with aggressive crawl changes the meaning of historical scores, so any trendline or clearance gating built on prior homepage-only results becomes apples-to-oranges unless the report schema/versioning is explicitly revised.

objections.title: Agent ownership is unresolved
objections.detail: The proposal says Agent #21 owns the Aggressive Crawl Conductor role, but also states it is dormant with no class file shipped and no `registerAgent()` call wired. Wiring aggressive crawl first without canonical agent registration creates a governance hole: the system would be using a capability that the SSOT treats as owned by an unshipped agent, which risks bypassing the agent-layer accountability model in §15.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: If assessment is switched to the full crawl before auth handling and agent registration are in place, teams may get slower, more expensive runs that still miss gated content because logins fail silently. That is worse than the current homepage-only output because it looks more authoritative while actually being noisier, costlier, and more likely to produce false confidence on private or authenticated product surfaces.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The strongest case for rejecting or deferring the proposal is that it conflates a crawl-engine enhancement with a production assessment contract change. Until authenticated traversal, canonical Agent #21 registration, and report/version compatibility are all settled, shipping this as the new assessment path risks breaking score comparability, operational budgets, and governance traceability. A pause for a foundation audit would reduce the chance of compounding hidden gaps into the scoring and clearance pipeline.

Q1.pick_text: Implementation gap — SSOT is sound; wire the engine that already exists.
Q1.rationale: The artifact explicitly describes a real multi-page `aggressiveCrawl()` implementation and a mismatch in wiring, not a contradiction in the SSOT’s intended behavior. The missing pieces are execution path, auth traversal, and agent registration, which are implementation concerns.

Q2.pick_text: Defect — single-page output must not be presented as a product assessment until the full-product crawl is wired.
Q2.rationale: Because the shipped assessment output is homepage-only while §6 specifies full-product coverage, presenting it as a complete product assessment is misleading. It may be acceptable as an internal diagnostic, but not as the claimed assessment artifact.

Q3.pick_text: Wire Agent #21 Ops Runner Alpha canonically first — per the SSOT §15.1 ownership row, not as a code shortcut around the agent layer.
Q3.rationale: The SSOT assigns ownership of the aggressive crawl conductor role to Agent #21, so bypassing that layer would create governance drift. Canonical registration first gives the later crawl wiring a legitimate owner and audit trail.

Q4.pick_text: Partial — only crawl-independent dormant agents before; crawl-dependent ones after the substrate exists.
Q4.rationale: Agents whose charters do not depend on full-product crawl can be built in parallel, but crawl-dependent agents should wait for the substrate they consume. That avoids rework while preserving progress on independent capabilities.

Q5.pick_text: Authenticated-traversal security: credential storage, session bleed, accidental data exfiltration via crawl.
Q5.rationale: Once authenticated traversal is added, the crawler will handle session-bearing fetches and possibly sensitive internal content. The main unmitigated risk is mishandling credentials or crossing tenant/session boundaries during broad crawl sweeps.

Q6.pick_text: Proceed in defined phases with explicit gates — staged build, each phase Panel-or-CEO-reviewed before the next.
Q6.rationale: A staged approach best balances urgency with governance. It lets the team first register Agent #21, then add authenticated traversal, then switch assessment over once the new path has been validated against the old one.

perReviewer.overallNotes: The proposal is directionally right about the gap, but it is under-scoped if treated as a simple wiring task. The safe path is phased delivery with explicit compatibility and security gates.

objections.title: §6 crawl scope vs crawler.js wiring

objections.title: §15.1 row 21 Agent #21 dormant

objections.title: §7.6 GTM Readiness scoring invalid
objections.detail: §7.6 defines the 100 − 10·crit − 5·high − 2·med − 0.5·low formula and four score bands that map to Clearance Step 5, yet all shipped assessment outputs derive from single-page homepage crawls, so the metric has never been validated on the multi-page input it assumes.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: Wiring the full-product engine without authenticated traversal first will emit multi-page reports that silently omit gated content, creating a false completeness signal that is harder to correct than the current explicit single-page limitation and erodes user trust faster than the status quo.
adversarial.precedent: Early Sauce Labs and BrowserStack full-site crawlers promised exhaustive authenticated coverage but delivered only partial unauthenticated snapshots on SPAs, producing misleading audit reports that required years of retrofits and damaged platform credibility.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The proposal's framing as a pure implementation gap understates that §6's authenticated multi-page + AI-probe contract exceeds the current single-page architecture by an order of magnitude; proceeding without a foundation audit risks compounding the three already-identified 'sounds-done-but-isn't' gaps into systemic rework once the 20 dormant agents begin consuming the new substrate.
